name: Design a Multi-Region Active-Active System
intent: Serve users from the nearest of several regions that all accept writes, keep the copies converging, survive the loss of a whole region, and keep each country's data where the law says it must stay.
codeTitle: last-writer-wins against a counter CRDT across three regions
finalIntro: One user liking a post from Frankfurt, and the like reaching the other regions.
prompt: Design the backend of a social app with 200 million users in North America, Europe and Asia. Every region must accept reads and writes so that users get fast responses everywhere. If a region fails, its users move to another one without data loss they can notice. European accounts must be stored in Europe.
functional: Route each user to a nearby region for reads and writes
Replicate every write to the other regions
Resolve two regions changing the same data at the same time
Fail over to another region when one is lost, and fail back later
Keep data of regulated users inside their region
Let a user see their own change right after making it
nonFunctional: Reads and writes complete in under 100 ms from the user's nearest region
Survive the loss of one full region with an availability of 99.99%
Replication lag between regions stays under about a second at the 99th percentile
No acknowledged write is silently lost, apart from the narrow window of an unreplicated tail at a region crash
All regions converge to the same state once the network heals
European personal data is never stored outside Europe

firstAttempt.text: One region, in the US, with an application tier and a primary database. Every user in the world connects to it. A second region holds a read-only copy for backup, to be switched on by hand if the first one fails.
limits: A user in Singapore pays about 200 ms of round trip for every request, and a page of five requests takes a second
The backup region sits idle, so half the money buys nothing until a disaster, and the switch has never been tested
When the US region fails, every user is down until someone promotes the backup, and the last seconds of writes are gone
European data lives in a US database, which breaks the data residency rules
The one primary is a single bottleneck for all write traffic in the world

steps.title: Put a full stack in each region and route users to the nearest
steps.problem: Light in fibre needs about 70 ms to cross the Atlantic one way and about 100 ms to reach Asia from the US, so no amount of tuning makes a single-region service fast for the whole world.
steps.fix: Run an independent copy of the whole stack, the application servers and a database, in each region, all serving live traffic. A global routing layer sends each user to the closest healthy region, using latency-based DNS or an anycast address that the network steers to the nearest point of presence. Within a region the usual load balancers spread the work, and every region is sized to be able to take over some of the others' load.
steps.tradeoff: Users get local latency and every region does useful work all the time, so there is no idle standby. Each region now has its own copy of the data, and the rest of the design is about keeping those copies consistent.

steps.title: Replicate every write to the other regions, asynchronously
steps.problem: A write accepted in Frankfurt must eventually be visible in Virginia and Singapore, but waiting for both to confirm would put an intercontinental round trip of 100 to 200 ms into every write.
steps.fix: A write is committed in the local region's database and acknowledged to the user at once. Its change record then goes onto a replication stream, with a sequence number per source region, to every other region, where it is applied in order. Each region remembers how far it has applied each peer's stream, so after an outage it resumes from that position and nothing is skipped or applied twice. Applying a record is made idempotent.
steps.tradeoff: Writes stay as fast as a single-region write, and a slow or broken link does not stop the other regions. The price is replication lag, typically between 50 ms and a second, during which regions disagree, and a window of recent writes that exist only in one region if that region is destroyed.

steps.title: Decide what happens when two regions write the same data
steps.problem: If a user edits a profile in Paris while their phone, on a different route, edits it in Virginia, each region accepts its own write, and the two changes meet only later, with no way to tell which one is right.
steps.fix: Pick the rule per kind of data. The simplest is last-writer-wins, where each write carries a timestamp from a hybrid logical clock and the higher one survives, with the region id breaking ties. Counters, sets and collaborative lists use CRDTs, whose merge function combines both changes without losing either, so two likes become two likes. Data that cannot be merged, such as a bank balance or a unique username, is given a home region that handles all writes for it, and other regions forward their writes there.
steps.tradeoff: Local writes always succeed and the regions converge without coordination. Last-writer-wins silently throws away one of two concurrent writes, and a wall clock that is slow by 100 ms can make an older write win, which is why a hybrid logical clock is used. CRDTs lose nothing but need a data model made for them, and a home region adds a cross-ocean hop for the users who are far from it.

steps.title: Detect a regional failure and fail over automatically
steps.problem: When a region dies, its users keep sending requests to it until something notices, and a person deciding at three in the morning whether to switch takes minutes to hours.
steps.fix: Health checks run from several outside locations against each region's public endpoints, and the routing layer takes a region out of rotation only when most checkers agree, which avoids reacting to one broken link. Users of the failed region are sent to the nearest remaining one, which already holds a copy of their data. The failed region is kept out of rotation, and the writes it had not yet replicated are recovered from its logs after it returns. Failing back is done gradually, after the region has caught up, with a small share of traffic first.
steps.tradeoff: Recovery takes tens of seconds instead of hours, and the failover path is used often enough to stay trusted. The surviving regions need spare capacity, roughly one extra region's worth spread across the others, and a mistaken failover under a flaky network can move load onto regions that cannot carry it.

steps.title: Keep regulated data in its home jurisdiction
steps.problem: Replicating every record everywhere would copy a European user's personal data to the US and Asia, which laws such as the GDPR and national data localisation rules can forbid.
steps.fix: Every record has a residency label taken from the account, such as 'EU'. A policy layer decides, per label, which regions may hold the record. EU-labelled personal data is written only to EU regions and its replication stream never leaves them, while a small pseudonymous reference, such as an opaque id, is all that the other regions store. The routing layer sends an EU user to an EU region even when a US one is closer, and failover for that user stays inside Europe, with at least two EU regions to fail between.
steps.tradeoff: The company can show where each piece of data lives and meet legal requirements. Some features, such as a global search over profiles, become harder, an EU user abroad sees extra latency for personal data, and a region pair must exist inside each regulated area, which raises cost.

steps.title: Show users their own writes despite replication lag
steps.problem: A user posts a comment in Frankfurt, and the next request is routed, after a network change, to a region the comment has not reached. The comment appears to have vanished, so the user posts it again.
steps.fix: Each write returns a version token, the per-region sequence numbers it depends on, which the client sends back with later reads. A region serves the read only if it has applied at least those positions, and otherwise it waits briefly, reads from the region that took the write, or redirects the user there. Users are normally kept on one region by session stickiness, and a lag monitor measures how far each region is behind so that the router can avoid a region whose lag is too large.
steps.tradeoff: Users never see their own changes disappear, while other people's changes can still arrive a moment late, which they cannot notice. A few reads wait or travel further, the tokens must be carried by every client, and the lag monitor has to be trusted.

failures.impact: A third of the users get errors, and the last second or so of writes accepted in that region has not left it.
failures.answer: Outside health checks agree it is down and the router moves its users to the next nearest region within tens of seconds, as the other regions already have the replicated data. The unreplicated tail stays in the failed region's logs and is merged back after it recovers, using the same conflict rules. Because the surviving regions run with spare capacity, they absorb the extra load, and the dashboards report the exact lag at the time of failure so the possible loss is known.

failures.scenario: The link between two regions is cut but both are up
failures.impact: Each side keeps accepting writes and the same data is changed on both sides, a split brain for everything without a single owner.
failures.answer: Active-active chooses availability: both sides keep serving, and the conflict rules merge the changes once the link returns. Data with a home region stops accepting writes where the home region cannot be reached, because a unique name or a balance must not be given out twice. The replication streams resume from the saved positions, and a background comparison of the regions' data finds and repairs any difference that remains.

failures.scenario: A region's clock runs 200 ms slow
failures.impact: With plain wall-clock last-writer-wins, a write made there loses to an older write from another region, so a user's newer edit is undone.
failures.answer: Timestamps come from a hybrid logical clock, which never moves backwards and jumps ahead to any timestamp it has seen, so a write made after seeing another always sorts after it. Clock offset is monitored and alarmed, and a server whose offset passes a limit is taken out of service. Data that cannot tolerate even this uses a home region instead.

failures.scenario: A bad write or a bug replicates everywhere
failures.impact: Active-active copies mistakes just as faithfully as good data, so a deleted table is deleted in every region within a second.
failures.answer: Replication is not a backup. Point-in-time backups and a delayed copy let the data be restored to before the mistake, and dangerous operations are rolled out region by region with a pause between them, so the first region can be stopped before the rest receive it.

alternatives.title: How regions share the work

options.name: Active-passive
options.pro: One writer, so no conflicts, and the simplest to reason about
options.con: The standby is idle, far users stay slow, and failover is slow and rarely tested

options.name: Active-active for reads, one write region
options.pro: Fast reads everywhere with no write conflicts
options.con: Every write crosses an ocean for far users, and failover of the writer is still needed

options.name: Active-active with writes everywhere
options.pro: Local latency for reads and writes and no idle capacity
options.con: Needs conflict rules, and lag is visible to users

alternatives.pick: Active-active everywhere, with a home region for the few kinds of data that cannot be merged.

alternatives.title: How conflicts are resolved

options.name: Last-writer-wins by wall clock
options.con: Drops concurrent writes and obeys skewed clocks

options.name: Last-writer-wins by hybrid logical clock
options.pro: Respects cause and effect and survives clock skew
options.con: Still drops one of two concurrent writes

options.name: CRDTs
options.pro: Merges without loss and without coordination
options.con: Needs data types designed for it, and history can grow

options.name: Home region per record
options.pro: Strong rules, no conflicts, and works for balances and unique names
options.con: Remote users pay a round trip, and the home region is a dependency

alternatives.pick: A hybrid logical clock by default, CRDTs for counters and sets, and a home region for money and unique keys.

alternatives.title: How replicas agree

options.name: Asynchronous replication
options.con: A lag window and a possible small loss at a crash

options.name: Synchronous replication to a quorum of regions
options.pro: No loss and a single order of writes
options.con: Every write pays a cross-region round trip, and losing two regions stops writes

alternatives.pick: Asynchronous replication for most data, and a quorum across regions only for the small set of records where loss is unacceptable.

alternatives.title: How routing finds the region

options.name: Latency-based DNS
options.pro: Simple and works with any client
options.con: Cached answers delay a failover by the time to live

options.name: Anycast
options.pro: Fast reroute when a region disappears, with no caches in the way
options.con: Needs a network provider and can split one user's traffic between regions

options.name: A smart client with a region list
options.pro: The client can retry elsewhere at once
options.con: Only works for apps you control and need updating

alternatives.pick: Anycast or low-TTL DNS at the edge, with the app retrying another region on error.

quiz.question: A social app runs in Virginia, Frankfurt and Singapore, and the target is a write completed in under 50 ms from the nearest region. The round trip from Frankfurt to Virginia is about 90 ms and to Singapore about 160 ms. How should a write made in Frankfurt be replicated?
options: Commit it in Frankfurt and acknowledge it, then ship it on a sequenced stream to the other regions
Wait for Virginia to confirm before acknowledging, since two of three regions already form a majority of the cluster
Wait for both other regions to confirm, so that every region holds the write before the user is told it succeeded
Send every write to Virginia as the single writer, and have Frankfurt answer reads from its own local copy of the data
quiz.explanation: Any wait on another region costs at least 90 ms on top of local work, which breaks the 50 ms goal, so the write is acknowledged locally and replicated asynchronously. The price is a lag window and a small unreplicated tail if Frankfurt is destroyed. A single writer in Virginia makes every Frankfurt write pay the same ocean crossing.

quiz.question: Users in three regions like the same post at the same moment. The like count is stored as one number, and conflicts are settled by last-writer-wins with a hybrid logical clock. Two regions each read 100 and write 101, and the count ends at 101 instead of 102. Likes must stay fast to write in every region. What is the best change?
options: Give each post a home region that handles all its likes, and forward likes from other regions there
Switch to a plain wall clock with a tighter NTP sync, so that the truly latest write is chosen more accurately
Make the count a CRDT counter, so each region adds its own increments and the merge sums them without losing any
Replicate likes synchronously to all regions, so that every increment reads the latest count before it writes
quiz.explanation: Last-writer-wins keeps one of two concurrent writes by design, whatever the clock, so a counter built on it loses increments. A CRDT counter merges both changes without coordination and keeps local writes fast. A home region would work but sends far users across an ocean for every like, and synchronous replication adds the same latency to every write.

quiz.question: A bad migration in Frankfurt drops a table of user settings. Within a second the change replicates to Virginia and Singapore, and all three copies are empty. The team had assumed three live regions meant three safe copies. Which measures protect against this kind of mistake?
options: Replicate synchronously to a quorum of regions, so that a destructive change must be confirmed by two regions before it applies
Keep point-in-time backups, and roll risky changes out one region at a time with a pause between regions
Fail users over to Virginia, whose copy of the settings table is still intact and can serve them while Frankfurt is repaired
Store the settings as CRDT types, so that the merge of the three copies brings back the rows that one region deleted
quiz.explanation: Replication copies mistakes as faithfully as good data, so recovery needs point-in-time backups, and staged rollouts limit how far a bad change travels. Synchronous replication would spread the drop even faster, Virginia's copy is already gone, and a CRDT merge would apply the delete too.
